Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

In Western music theory, the standard pitch has changed several times over the years. Today it is 440 Hz, written A440: the A above middle C. In 1939 an international conference proposed fixing the A above middle C at 440 hertz. In 1955 the International Organization for Standardization adopted this as ISO 16 (and reaffirmed it in 1975). Since then, A440 has been the reference for tuning pianos, violins and other instruments.

Search for “432 Hz” on any video site and you will find plenty of videos that retune all kinds of music to a reference pitch of 432 Hz, because some people think 432 Hz simply sounds better.

For others, though, retuning is about more than taste. Some blogs claim that standard 440 Hz tuning is bad for your health. But could your imagination ever stretch far enough to drag the Nazis into this?

“The recent rediscoveries of the vibratory / oscillatory nature of the universe indicate that this contemporary international concert pitch standard may generate an unhealthy effect or anti-social behavior in the consciousness of human beings … There is a theory that the change from 432 Hz to 440 Hz was dictated by Nazi propaganda minister, Joseph Goebbels” [1]

A listening test

To find out how people actually perceive different reference pitches, Professor Trevor Cox of the University of Salford decided to run a series of online tests. Health effects are hard to assess, so the test focused on subjective preference, which is also what drives all those YouTubers posting comparison videos. The ten pieces of music came from the Free Music Archive, and some of them differed very strongly in character. Each piece was tuned to a different reference pitch: 416, 424, 432, 440, 448, 456 and 465 Hz. Listeners only had to say which tuning they preferred. Several hundred people took part, and 1,396 trials were completed.

The preference results are shown below.

Preference for different reference pitches

A higher mean means listeners liked the music more at that reference pitch. Clearly, the reference pitch has a significant effect on preference (confirmed statistically with a Kruskal–Wallis test, p < 0.001). Tuning the music up made it sound worse (p < 0.03, Mann–Whitney U test), whereas tuning it down did not affect preference much.

People might expect music retuned to 432 Hz to sound nicer, or even to be better music. In the experiment, however, average preference actually dropped slightly when the pitch was lowered. Perhaps when we listen to music we pay more attention to relative pitch, though that may not hold for people with perfect pitch. The drop in preference for raised pitch may also be due to artifacts of the pitch-shifting method used in the experiment.

Test time!

The video below plays four pieces of music, each tuned to both 440 Hz and 432 Hz. Have a listen: do you prefer A or B? The answer is revealed at the end of the video.

Next, a Coldplay classic, “The Scientist.” Compare the two versions: which do you like better?

440 Hz version

432 Hz version

I bet anyone who knows this song won’t make it to the end of the 432 Hz version: it just feels like it’s lost its punch. Of course, a lot of that comes down to the processing, and the 432 Hz version seems to have more processing artifacts.

So what about music that hasn’t been digitally pitch-shifted at all, where the instruments themselves were tuned differently? How does that sound to you?

(Forgive the dreadful audio quality after video compression…)

Personally, I can hear the difference in every piece except the second to last. Pay attention to the last two: the second to last is Pink Floyd’s “Wish You Were Here,” and the last is Ed Sheeran’s “I See Fire.” The Floyd song is mostly low notes, with the first few around one or two hundred hertz, while the Sheeran song sits much higher. According to Zwicker’s Psychoacoustics, below 500 Hz we can at best distinguish two pure tones 1 Hz apart; above 500 Hz the resolution is roughly 0.002 times the frequency [5]. Clearly my own resolution below 500 Hz is a good deal coarser than 8 Hz -_-

Which version do you prefer?
